cues.text: A Theft by a Former Altar Boy
On November 5, 1824, in Onil, a town in Spain’s Valencia region roughly twenty-four miles north of Alicante, Nicolas Bernabeu stole the monstrance holding the Blessed Sacrament.
He also stole other liturgical objects belonging to the parish church of St. James the Apostle, where he had once served as an altar boy.
Days later, a woman from the nearby town of Tibi came upon the stolen pyx, still holding the consecrated Host, lying in the middle of a green field, entirely undisturbed.
She carried it back to Onil herself, where the townspeople received her with a celebration befitting the return of what they had feared lost for good.
The Host remained enshrined in the parish church, its preservation drawing periodic attention over the following century.
On November 28, 1943 — exactly 119 years after the theft — Don Guillermo Hijarrubia acted as delegate of the Archbishop of Valencia.
He formally confirmed the relic’s authenticity and verified that the Host remained completely preserved, without any sign of decay ordinarily expected after so long a span.
A chapel was built on the site where the woman from Tibi discovered the stolen pyx.
The story’s stages are depicted today in St. James Church in Onil’s stained-glass windows, giving visitors a visual record of the theft, discovery, and the Host’s return.
The relic's feast is kept locally each year from November 24 through 30.

By the time of its most recent examinations, the Host recovered from that green field near Tibi had remained intact for close to two centuries, a span its own preservation gives no ordinary explanation for.
The Onil tradition, like several others in this same period of Spanish Eucharistic devotion, centers not on transformation or vision.
Instead, it centers on simple, sustained physical survival—a theft undone not by the thief's capture, but by a single stranger's decision to carry what she had found back to the town it belonged to.
